summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in January 1983. Replaced by RFC 837.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

subtitle: January 1983 snapshot of TCP service adoption across early Internet hosts.

tldr.problem: TCP adoption across the Internet was still unevenly distributed, and no recent data existed on which hosts could accept connections.
tldr.mechanism: David Smallberg ran the same survey as RFC 835 in early January 1983, testing connectivity to Telnet, FTP, and SMTP across 315 hosts from the NIC hostname table.
tldr.outcome: The survey showed increased adoption: 91 hosts now accepted Telnet, 70 accepted FTP, and 72 accepted SMTP, demonstrating steady growth over the month since the previous survey. This edition was replaced by RFC 837 with data from mid-January.

today: RFC 837 published an updated survey one week later with data from January 11-12, 1983, replacing these early-January results.

sections.title: An Updated Survey of TCP Services
sections.content:
RFC 836 is an updated survey by David Smallberg, repeating the methodology of RFC 835 but with data from January 1983. The survey tested 315 hosts for their ability to accept Telnet, FTP, and SMTP connections via TCP.

The tests ran from January 4 to 5, 1983, with failed and problematic hosts retried on January 5. This survey used the NIC hostname table dated December 20, 1982, as its host list.
sections.eli5: A month later, the same researcher knocked on the same computers to see the current state of TCP adoption.

sections.title: Survey Methodology and Classification
sections.content:
The survey uses the same methodology as RFC 835: hosts are classified by their claimed capabilities in the hostname table, then tested to see whether they accept connections. Results are recorded as accepted, refused, unreachable, dead, or no service offered.

The RFC presents summary tables showing the counts of each result type for each service, followed by detailed alphabetical and host-table-order listings of every host and its specific results.
sections.eli5: Same method as before: check the claims, try to connect, and record what happens.

sections.title: Growth in TCP Adoption
sections.content:
Adoption grew significantly month-to-month: 91 hosts now accepted Telnet (up from 61 in December), 70 accepted FTP (up from 43), and 72 accepted SMTP (up from 44). The total number of hosts claiming TCP capabilities also grew, from 314 to 315 hosts surveyed. Notably, more hosts claiming services now actually delivered them, suggesting either deployment had accelerated or the previous survey under-reported working services.

Unreachability and dead hosts remained a significant factor: many systems were still not connected or were offline during testing.
sections.eli5: About 50 percent more hosts answered for Telnet and email this month. This shows TCP was spreading quickly across the network.

sections.title: Comparative Analysis from Monthly Data
sections.content:
Comparing RFC 836 to RFC 835 shows clear deployment momentum: Telnet support increased 49 percent (61 to 91 hosts), FTP increased 63 percent (43 to 70), and SMTP increased 64 percent (44 to 72). The growth was not uniform across the network; some major computing centers remained unreachable, while others had come online or activated services.

The data demonstrates that TCP service deployment was accelerating in the early months of 1983, driven by increasing Internet connectivity and broader adoption of TCP-based protocols. Major research centers and computing facilities were moving toward offering these services as standard capabilities.
sections.eli5: Every service was growing at the same fast rate, meaning the whole network was adopting TCP together. It was like a wave spreading across the system.
